about.title: Adding and Subtracting Polynomials
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. This class has two jobs: naming polynomials, then adding and subtracting them. Each idea gets its own short step. You can pause after the standard form step and do the adding and subtracting later.

sources.title: 6.1 Add and Subtract Polynomials, Elementary Algebra
6.01: Add and Subtract Polynomials (OpenStax Elementary Algebra)
5.1 Add and Subtract Polynomials, Intermediate Algebra
HSA-APR.A.1 (Common Core standard: arithmetic with polynomials)

say.text: Welcome to class 33. Today we learn to name polynomials, then add and subtract them. Take your time, and pause whenever you like.
First, the big word. A polynomial is one monomial, or several monomials joined by adding or subtracting.
We name a polynomial by counting its terms. Terms are the pieces split apart by plus or minus signs. One term is a monomial, two is a binomial, three is a trinomial.

show.text: monomial = 1 term (example: 6x²) | binomial = 2 terms (example: x + 4) | trinomial = 3 terms (example: x² + 3x + 4)

ask.q: How many terms does x² + 8x − 10 have, and what is it called?
ask.why: The plus and minus signs split it into x², 8x and 10. That makes three terms, and three terms is a trinomial.

say.text: What about four or more terms? Those are just called polynomials. And every monomial, binomial and trinomial is also a polynomial.

show.text: Special names: monomial, binomial, trinomial | Everything else: just 'polynomial' (and the special ones are polynomials too)

ask.q: Is a single term like 7x² also a polynomial?
ask.right: Yes, every monomial is a polynomial
wrong: No, a polynomial needs two or more terms
Only if it has a plus sign
ask.why: A monomial is the smallest kind of polynomial. It has exactly one term.

say.text: Next idea: degree. The degree of a term is the sum of the exponents on its variables. So 8y² has degree 2.

show.text: degree of a term = sum of the exponents

ask.q: What is the degree of the term 5x³?
ask.why: The degree comes from the exponent, not the number in front. The exponent on x is 3, so the degree is 3.

say.text: Two small cases. A plain number like 14 has degree 0. And a lone letter like −13a has degree 1, because a is a to the first power. With two variables, add the exponents: 3 + 5 makes 8.

ask.q: What is the degree of the constant 14?
ask.why: A constant has no variable, so there are no exponents to add. The degree of any constant is 0.

say.text: Now the degree of a whole polynomial. Find the degree of each term. The biggest one wins.

show.text: degree of a polynomial = the highest degree of its terms

ask.why: The terms have degrees 4, 2 and 0. The highest is 4, so the polynomial has degree 4.

say.text: Now we can give a polynomial its full name. 5x³ − 2x has two terms and top degree 3. So it is a binomial of degree 3.

ask.q: What is the full name of 2x² + 7x − 1?
ask.why: It has three terms, so it is a trinomial. The highest exponent is 2, so the degree is 2.

say.text: One more habit. Standard form means writing the terms from the highest degree down to the lowest. It makes polynomials easier to work with.

ask.q: Which polynomial is written in standard form?
ask.why: The degrees go 3, 2, 1, 0, from highest to lowest. The other lists jump around or run from lowest to highest.

say.text: Naming is done. Now we add. Adding polynomials is just combining like terms. 3 blocks plus 2 blocks make 5 blocks, and 3x plus 2x makes 5x.
Like terms have the same variable with the same exponent. 5x² and −2x² are like terms and make 3x². But 3x and 3x² are different, so they can't be added.

show.text: Like terms: 5x² + (−2x²) = 3x² | Not like terms: 3x and 3x² stay separate

ask.why: Only 6x² and −4x² have the same variable and the same exponent. In the other pairs, either the variable or the exponent is different.

say.text: Here is the recipe for adding. Drop the parentheses. Put like terms together. Combine them.

show.text: 1. Drop the parentheses | 2. Rearrange so like terms sit together | 3. Combine like terms

say.text: Let's try it. (3x² + 5x + 2) + (x² − 2x + 4). Group the x² terms, the x terms and the plain numbers. That gives 4x² + 3x + 6.

ask.why: Add the numbers in front of matching terms: 2 + 3 = 5, 1 + 4 = 5 and 1 + 5 = 6. The exponents stay the same, so x² stays x².

say.text: Now subtraction, which needs more care with signs. First, a warm-up. Subtracting a negative acts like adding. So 9n − (−5n) becomes 9n + 5n, which is 14n.

ask.why: Subtracting −6q is the same as adding 6q. So 12q + 6q = 18q.

say.text: Now the big rule. When you subtract a polynomial, the minus sign hits every term inside the parentheses. Flip every sign. This is the step people most often miss.

ask.q: What is the correct first step for (5x + 3) − (2x − 1)?
ask.why: The minus sign flips both terms in the second parentheses. 2x becomes −2x, and −1 becomes +1.

say.text: A bigger one: (9w² − 7w + 5) − (2w² − 4). Flip the signs, then combine. The second polynomial has no w term, so −7w just stays as it is.

ask.why: Flip the signs to get 6m² + 3m + 8 − 2m² + 5. Then 6m² − 2m² = 4m², 3m stays, and 8 + 5 = 13.

say.text: A game example. Say a game shop's revenue is 5x² + 20x dollars and its costs are 2x² + 8x + 30. Profit is revenue minus costs.

ask.q: In that example, what is the profit polynomial?
ask.why: Flip every sign in the costs. Then 5x² − 2x² = 3x², 20x − 8x = 12x, and 0 − 30 = −30.

say.text: Why does this always work out neatly? Add or subtract two polynomials and you get another polynomial. The family stays closed, like integers under adding and subtracting.

ask.q: If you subtract one polynomial from another, what do you get?
wrong: Something that is never a polynomial
ask.why: Polynomials are closed under addition and subtraction. The result is always another polynomial.

say.text: Let's put it together. Name it, add or subtract with care, and finish in standard form. Mistakes here are normal, and checking each sign is a good habit.

show.text: 1. Count terms: mono-, bi-, tri- | 2. Find the degree: the highest | 3. Subtracting? Flip every sign in the second polynomial | 4. Combine like terms | 5. Write in standard form
